Bush racing

By: Annalise Lubbe | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
It is known as bush riding - a brutal and inhumane sport organised by gangsters that forces retired racehorses to run themselves literally to death. Carte Blanche investigates.

Unique Selling Point:
Retired race horses are forced to run beyond their limits on tar roads, often around blocks of houses leading to severe animal cruelty and abuse. Controlled by gangs and suspected ringleaders the sport of bush racing has been difficult to crack down by law enforcement. The SPCA lacks the funds and so this inhumane sport continues to grow in the Western Cape amongst the coloured communities.


Summary:
It was the Wednesday before Easter Weekend. When most families were getting ready to celebrate this special time of the year, Michael Brand was in a state of anxiety. He bought a horse from Jenny Middleton who runs a rehoming centre for retired race horses in Phillip on the Cape Flats last Saturday. Max was a six year old mare in good shape and there was an immediate bond between the two. Michael was eager to fetch Max that Saturday. But then his plans went astray when he got a call from Jenny saying that Max was missing. The fence of the property was cut and both Max and another horse, named Wavin Flag was taken. Jenny’s immediate fear was that the horses were stolen for bush racing.

With a large bush racing meeting scheduled for the Cape Flats over easter weekend, fears ran high that the horses had been stolen for illicit racing. Michael got onto social media and with the news shared on various platforms and the help of SAPS stock theft unit, a PI and drone surveillance footage Max and Wavin Flag was eventually found on Easter Friday in the dunes of Rocklands near Mitchells Plain. The recovery team was surrounded by a fairly hostile crowd of people leading to further speculation that the racing might have been linked to gangs who run the horses for bets, akin to cock fighting and dog figiting rings.

When Michael saw Max his fears were confirmed. “Max could not even get into the horse box by himself, it took 10 of us to load him in,” he remembers. Back at the centre Jenny was waiting with a vet to attend to the animals. “They’d obviously been galloped into the ground” says Jenny as their mouths had wires through them and were bleeding and you could see straightaway that Max’s leg did not look good.” X Rays revealed that Max had sustained serious injuries, including fracturing his sesamoids beyond repair and due to the extent of his injuries the decision was made to euthanise him humanely.


Further information:
Michael still gets choked up when he thinks about what Max must have gone through. This is the story of so many cases involving bush racing - a secretive sport that has been difficult to crack down.

The sport has become a highly lucrative pastime for weekends and public holidays and is rife across the coloured communities of the Western Cape. The location is kept a secret till the last moment to ensure no unwanted parties will interfere as horses are often stolen and shows signs of severe animal abuse. It is known that this form of sport puts horses through the most severe tests in order to win the race. There are no rules, no regulations, only the prize money at stake for the winner.

The horses are transported in the most inhumane way. Tied by ropes they are stacked on top of another at the back of a bakkie and taken to the location. Once at the race, no proper equipment is used. Instead, a wire bit in the mouth for control, a shambock or teaser for speed, and bare-back riding, causing severe friction and sores in the process.

And the racecourse? The veld or a backstreet tar road filled with litter and debris causing major injuries in the horse’s hooves. Evidence of this is found in a veterinary report from Dr. John Midgley from Atlantis area when he examined a severely traumatised horse that was found after a bush race that came in with multiple injuries. She had open sores, bruises on her back and abscesses on her hooves. ‘The abscess on her hooves is from working at speed for an extended period of time on hard surfaces such as tar roads,” Midgley stated.

And when a horse is no longer able to run, the owners simply abandon the animal in the veld left to die. Alma Schaap from African Tails, who works with the communities of the Swartland area through offering animal rescue services will tell you how often she has been called by a local community member who found a dead horse close to where bush racing has taken place. Alma has held workshops with the community members where she tried to install a sense of responsibility towards the horse’s welfare. It has been a long journey and she has seen some results but in most cases the abuse is at the hands of gangsters who simply don’t care, she states.

What concerns her is that very little has been done by the authorities over the years. She has on numerous occasions informed the SPCA about a bush race in their area when she hears about it via an informer but no real action has been taken she feels, not by them nor by SAPS in trying to rescue these animals from severe abuse. Often it is a case of not enough manpower and a lack of funds they say.

And when you ask about where the horses come from, Alma will tell you that are either stolen or sold by a local farmer in the Swartberg, called Visser. He drops off a bunch of horses every now and then in Mamre and these people buy a retired racehorse for as little as R500, she says.

Alma works closely with equestrian community who has helped with rescue horses in building them up to strength again. Anushka, seen by Dr. Midgley was a worse case scenario that took 6 months to heal from open sores and injuries she sustained in races. Today she is at a happy home and shows new life again. But so many of these horses are not rescued in time and the spiral of abuse continue.

Our story:
Through the eyes of Michael we will hear about Max’s story in Mitchells Plain and show the drone footage of the rescue mission. There is also supporting go-pro visuals of Max at the rehoming centre and some of the team members who worked together during the rescue mission.

A visit to the heart of the Swartland, Atlantis, Pella and Mamre, where many of these events are held over weekends will form part of our story. You only need to visit the coloured community of Mamre to spot a horse in the backyard that is severely neglected to know what his purpose is, as Alma will testify.

We will send a drone camera into the town of Mamre this weekend during the annual flower show as there is a planned race on the Saturday we were told. We hope to get aerial visuals of this event as it is virtually impossible for one of us to get ground visuals during the event without putting our lives at risk. The race is 100% coloured community attending.

We aim to find Farmer Visser and see if he will speak to us about the horses he sells to the coloureds for bush racing. If we are able to get one of the locals who bought a horse from farmer Visser the story will be stronger.

We will get a spokesperson of the SPCA and Law Enforcement representative to talk to us about what action they have taken and how they intend to stamp out bush racing.

The veterinary report and an interview with the Dr. will form part of the evidence of one of the horses, Anuschka, who is now in good hands and recovering. This I feel is also important for our viewers to feel it is not all doom and gloom but that there is a shimmer of hope for those horses that are rescued.

In closing, this is an extremely difficult story to get ground visuals of so most of the evidence will be from drone footage as well as a cellphone recording of a race given to us by someone from the horse cart association who cannot go on camera as she fears for her safety.

Press Release:


Bush Racing
Bush racing has become a popular underground pastime in which retired race horses are literally raced to their
death. It’s a brutal sport run by gangs across the Western Cape for gambling purposes. Carte Blanche asks: why has
law enforcement failed to put an end to this cruel sport?

Script:


Script: Bush racing
5 October 2017
Duration: 10min

V/O It was Easter weekend when Garth Malpass, an avid drone enthusiast, received a call from a friend asking for help. Two of her horses, Max an Wavin Flag were stolen from her stables in the Philippi area of the Cape Flats and she was desperate to find them. It was the second day of the search with no sign of the animals. On board were a PI, a SAPS stock theft unit officer and concerned members of the equine community.

Link: There was only so much that the search party could do from the road. But what they really needed was an eye in the sky which is why they turned to drone technology.

Garth Malpass: Drone pilot: So I joined them that Saturday morning about 7am and we followed through the cape flats area but in a rush, it was go, go, go because time was of the essence.

V/O There was a growing concern amongst the search party that the horses were stolen for the purpose of illicit bush racing.

Garth Malpass: We were in the Mitchells plain area. As it was up in the air more and more people were crowding us, the gangs came up to us, I was feeling uncomfortable. It was definitely overwhelming, you never know what is going to happen.

V/O Malpass circled the drone a few times, desperate to find the animals before the situation on the ground gets out of hand. Then he spotted Max and Wavin Flag in the distance with 5 youngsters.

Garth Malpass: I could see the one horse was limping. As they came over the hill we saw the horse was really bad, they were run down they looked exhausted.

V/O Three days prior Max and Wavin Flag were in perfect condition. The only feasible explanation for their injuries was that the animals have been run into the ground in bush racing.

John: So, the condition of the one horse was so bad it had to be helped?

Garth Malpass: Not only was it a broken leg, it was shaking so much as if it wanted to fall over and we were keeping it up. It was very very sad.

Up natural sound

V/O Bush racing is a game of no rules. The locals call it dicing. Unlike formal horse racing where the surface is specially designed for horses, bush racing and dicing takes place on hard surfaces and even on tar roads. The location changes often to avoid unwanted attention. And the riders are youngsters who have no proper training or riding gear. There are no vet on standby to check their condition of the horses. From Mitchells Plain to Delft and Atlantis, the sport has become synonymous with the shadowy world of drugs, illegal gambling, gangsters and thieves.

Oscar Pick: Hulle is met sangsters en guns en hulle kom met gevaarlike weapons en ons kan nie die ding hok slaan nie. (they are with gangsters and guns and they come with dangerous weapons. We cannot stop this.)

Up natural sound

V/O Oscar is a horse owner and breeder from the Mamre community. He has been threatened by gangsters and keeps his horses locked behind solid doors to prevent them from being stolen.

Oscar Pick: Horse owner: Die polisie se vir jou ok kom ons kyk of ons die perd kan kry. (The police says ok, let’s look if we can find the horse) Dan kry jy weer die perd, somtyds vandag somtyds more, (then you find your horse again, sometimes today sometimes tomorrow) somtyds na n maand maar dan is jou perd nie meer soos wat hy was nie (sometimes after a month but then your horse is not what it used to be). Hy’s maar hy is vol sere hy is gesny met die mes, die rug is stukkend. (he is thin, full of sores, cut with a knife, his back is broken) Hulle ry vir hom met draad in die mond, toue in die mond, hulle ry bloots. (they ride him with a wire in the mouth, string in the mouth, they ride him without a saddle)

V/O Reagon Fortuin’s horses are kept here on the same property as Oscar’s. Six weeks ago his horse Nicks was stolen from the property.

Up natural audio

Reagon Fortuin: Horse owner: Hy is nie naby die kondisie wat hy was toe ek hom gekry het, hy was so te se amper dood. (Subtitle: he is not nearly in the same condition as what he was when I found him, he was almost dead) Twee dae se ry en dis wat jy kry, voete seer, hy het skoene aangehad die skoene is afgery. (two days of riding, and this is what you get, sore feet, it had shoes on, the shoes are ridden off).

Up natural sound

V/O Dr. Jennifer Deverson, a veterinarian from the Swartland area has treated many horses she suspected had been involved in bush racing.

John Webb: Are there certain injuries, associated with racing and if so what are they ?

Dr. Jennifer Deverson; Bruising of the feet, abscesses, so the horse is sore they potentially get pain medicine from a friend, mask the pain, ride the horse again, so it gets worse and worse and that ongoing percussive injury leads to stress fractures. That is when you will see fractured limbs and really being ridden to the point of exhaustion.

John: What a horrendous experience.

Dr. Jennifer Deverson: So badly fitting tac. If its spine is exposed because it hasn't got enough muscle on it. It is going to create a sore that gets an infection in it. They will still ride that horse repeatedly. These horses are just ridden until they can't go any more.

V/O Mayanna Muter has helped many horses in distress over the years. She runs a small rescue centre here in Dassenberg in the Atlantis area and often get calls from owner to help animals in need of help.

Mayanna Muter: Horse rescue owner: Sadly I am not able to take animals away from their owners so what I had to do is to buy horses to get them away from to get them away from the environment they are in. The injuries, a lot of them have these massive wounds on their backs from constant friction, they have stab wounds, one horse was actually sliced. They don’t really give a darn what they do or how they do it. If the horse is a failure they will annihilate it if it is not a failure it continues with the abuse until it can no longer continue.

Audio natural sound

V/O Alma Schaap works for an animal welfare organization. Her work in the Pella, Mamre and Atlantis areas is mainly focused on the sterilization of pets but she cannot turn a blind eye when she sees the living conditions of many of the horses in these area.

John Webb: Where are they being kept, I assume they are not in stables?

Alma Schaap: Animal Welfare: a lot of them are tethered and a lot of them are tethered not in a humane way, tight ropes, nylon ropes that cut into their legs and things like that.

Link: The SPCA is the go-to organization when it comes to animal welfare. To do its job it is often required to work hand in glove with law enforcement and at times the SA police service.

V/O We requested an interview with SPCA Cape of Good Hope as Atlantis and Mamre falls under their jurisdiction. However in an email response CEO Allan Perrins said ‘bush racing may be an urban legend’ . But in this press release of 2013 his office “appealed to the public for assistance in clamping down on bush racing across the province.” Perrins referred us to SPCA Swartland. We spoke to their chairperson, Colette Mang.

John Webb: I am not quite understanding why the SPCA does not seem keen on admitting that racing is an issue.

Colette Mang: Oh it is an issue and we are totally opposed to racing but you have the racing, in order to fix that let's try and fix the cause. The other problem we had is we had our inspectors threatened. Our senior inspector had to to euthanize a horse and the gang member said to him I know who you are and I know where you stay. Now that is a scary thing to hear.

Link: The Mamre flower festival is held every September and is built as a fun filled day out for the entire family but as we discovered, it also has a sinister side.

V/O With the drone camera we were able to survey the territory. As the day progressed several groups of riders were warming up and gathering in the nearby fields. From the main road into Mamre, riders from Atlantis were entering. It was clear to us that the local community were accustomed to sharing the roads with the horses as they gave way to the animals. Schaap was at the flower show.

Alma Shaap: Animal Welfare: We could see the activity of the horses right near our stall, so close were they and it was mind blowing that where people were parking their cars, where children were walking, literally 60 horses would just come past you speeding in the road.

Link: Come late afternoon this stretch of the road was turned into an impromptu race course. We captured footage of two races but then was spotted by scouts and had to beat a hasty retreat.

V/O From the sky we could see no visible or definitive starting point or even a winning post. Over a stretch of about 4000 meters several riders were competing pushing their horses hard and fast. Here you can see one of the riders trying to pull his opponent off his horse. Bush racing lasts several days and when the horses can no longer perform, they are simply dumped.

John Webb: If it is that obvious that these races are happening why is the SPCA does not follow up?

Colette Mang: Yeah because we are a very small SPCA (long pause) we would need help. we haven't had a lot of support from Law enforcement.

V/O We put this to the deputy chief of Law Enforcement for the City of Cape Town.

John Webb: We have hear from people of the SPCA that if they do ask for intervention form law enforcement they don’t get a lot of support to bush racing in particular.

Leon Wentzel: Acting Deputy Chief Law Enforcement: City of Cape Town
With regards to bush racing as indicated, it is actually the first time we have encountered this or heard about it.

John Webb: If it is that obvious to us why is it not obvious to other people particularly law enforcement?

Leon Wentzel: All the dockets throughout the city gets processed by my officer, thus far it is the first time we encounter something like this.

V/O Back at Mamre, our drone circled the sky and on the ground parked on the ground parked at the bush race was a police vehicle, the occupants engaging in a conversation with one of the riders. They did not appear to make any effort in investigating what was clearly an illegal activity taking place.

John Webb: Another worrying aspect is that there are law enforcers present at these events. That is obviously something you will investigate?

Leon Wentzel: That would be and I will definitely initiate an investigation. We do not take it lightly when officers turn a blind eye to any contravention or where the safety of the public is concerned.

V/O Garth has become a strong supporter of animal rights and has spent more time in contributing to rescue missions with his drone.

Garth Malpass: The more I got into it the more emotional i got an the more I wanted to find these horses and the more I wanted to assist with.

V/O Of the two retired racehorses that were rescued over that Easter Weekend by Garth and his the team one did not make it. Max’s injuries was so severe that he was put to sleep.

V/O Bush racing is an inhumane sport organised by gangsters with total disregard for the welfare of the animal.

15 seconds:
V/O This is bush racing, a sport organised by gangsters who race the animals into the ground.
Mayanna Muter: The injuries, a lot of them have these massive wounds on their backs from constant friction, they have stab wounds, one horse was actually sliced.

15 seconds:
V/O In bush racing stolen horses are raced to their death.
Garth Malpass: Not only was it a broken leg, it was exhausted, it was shaking so much as if it wanted to fall over.
Jennifer Deverson: These horses are just ridden until they can't go any more.

It’s a brutal sport run by gangs across the Western Cape for gambling purposes. Carte Blanche asks: why has law enforcement failed to put an end to this cruel sport? Script: Script: Bush racing 5 October 2017 Duration: 10min V/O It was Easter weekend when Garth Malpass, an avid drone enthusiast, received a call from a friend asking for help. Two of her horses, Max an Wavin Flag were stolen from her stables in the Philippi area of the Cape Flats and she was desperate to find them. It was the second day of the search with no sign of the animals. On board were a PI, a SAPS stock theft unit officer and concerned members of the equine community. Link: There was only so much that the search party could do from the road. But what they really needed was an eye in the sky which is why they turned to drone technology. Garth Malpass: Drone pilot: So I joined them that Saturday morning about 7am and we followed through the cape flats area but in a rush, it was go, go, go because time was of the essence. V/O There was a growing concern amongst the search party that the horses were stolen for the purpose of illicit bush racing. Garth Malpass: We were in the Mitchells plain area. As it was up in the air more and more people were crowding us, the gangs came up to us, I was feeling uncomfortable. It was definitely overwhelming, you never know what is going to happen. V/O Malpass circled the drone a few times, desperate to find the animals before the situation on the ground gets out of hand. Then he spotted Max and Wavin Flag in the distance with 5 youngsters. Garth Malpass: I could see the one horse was limping. As they came over the hill we saw the horse was really bad, they were run down they looked exhausted. V/O Three days prior Max and Wavin Flag were in perfect condition. The only feasible explanation for their injuries was that the animals have been run into the ground in bush racing. John: So, the condition of the one horse was so bad it had to be helped? Garth Malpass: Not only was it a broken leg, it was shaking so much as if it wanted to fall over and we were keeping it up. It was very very sad. Up natural sound V/O Bush racing is a game of no rules. The locals call it dicing. Unlike formal horse racing where the surface is specially designed for horses, bush racing and dicing takes place on hard surfaces and even on tar roads. The location changes often to avoid unwanted attention. And the riders are youngsters who have no proper training or riding gear. There are no vet on standby to check their condition of the horses. From Mitchells Plain to Delft and Atlantis, the sport has become synonymous with the shadowy world of drugs, illegal gambling, gangsters and thieves. Oscar Pick: Hulle is met sangsters en guns en hulle kom met gevaarlike weapons en ons kan nie die ding hok slaan nie. (they are with gangsters and guns and they come with dangerous weapons. We cannot stop this.) Up natural sound V/O Oscar is a horse owner and breeder from the Mamre community. He has been threatened by gangsters and keeps his horses locked behind solid doors to prevent them from being stolen. Oscar Pick: Horse owner: Die polisie se vir jou ok kom ons kyk of ons die perd kan kry. (The police says ok, let’s look if we can find the horse) Dan kry jy weer die perd, somtyds vandag somtyds more, (then you find your horse again, sometimes today sometimes tomorrow) somtyds na n maand maar dan is jou perd nie meer soos wat hy was nie (sometimes after a month but then your horse is not what it used to be). Hy’s maar hy is vol sere hy is gesny met die mes, die rug is stukkend. (he is thin, full of sores, cut with a knife, his back is broken) Hulle ry vir hom met draad in die mond, toue in die mond, hulle ry bloots. (they ride him with a wire in the mouth, string in the mouth, they ride him without a saddle) V/O Reagon Fortuin’s horses are kept here on the same property as Oscar’s. Six weeks ago his horse Nicks was stolen from the property. Up natural audio Reagon Fortuin: Horse owner: Hy is nie naby die kondisie wat hy was toe ek hom gekry het, hy was so te se amper dood. (Subtitle: he is not nearly in the same condition as what he was when I found him, he was almost dead) Twee dae se ry en dis wat jy kry, voete seer, hy het skoene aangehad die skoene is afgery. (two days of riding, and this is what you get, sore feet, it had shoes on, the shoes are ridden off). Up natural sound V/O Dr. Jennifer Deverson, a veterinarian from the Swartland area has treated many horses she suspected had been involved in bush racing. John Webb: Are there certain injuries, associated with racing and if so what are they ? Dr. Jennifer Deverson; Bruising of the feet, abscesses, so the horse is sore they potentially get pain medicine from a friend, mask the pain, ride the horse again, so it gets worse and worse and that ongoing percussive injury leads to stress fractures. That is when you will see fractured limbs and really being ridden to the point of exhaustion. John: What a horrendous experience. Dr. Jennifer Deverson: So badly fitting tac. If its spine is exposed because it hasn't got enough muscle on it. It is going to create a sore that gets an infection in it. They will still ride that horse repeatedly. These horses are just ridden until they can't go any more. V/O Mayanna Muter has helped many horses in distress over the years. She runs a small rescue centre here in Dassenberg in the Atlantis area and often get calls from owner to help animals in need of help. Mayanna Muter: Horse rescue owner: Sadly I am not able to take animals away from their owners so what I had to do is to buy horses to get them away from to get them away from the environment they are in. The injuries, a lot of them have these massive wounds on their backs from constant friction, they have stab wounds, one horse was actually sliced. They don’t really give a darn what they do or how they do it. If the horse is a failure they will annihilate it if it is not a failure it continues with the abuse until it can no longer continue. Audio natural sound V/O Alma Schaap works for an animal welfare organization. Her work in the Pella, Mamre and Atlantis areas is mainly focused on the sterilization of pets but she cannot turn a blind eye when she sees the living conditions of many of the horses in these area. John Webb: Where are they being kept, I assume they are not in stables? Alma Schaap: Animal Welfare: a lot of them are tethered and a lot of them are tethered not in a humane way, tight ropes, nylon ropes that cut into their legs and things like that. Link: The SPCA is the go-to organization when it comes to animal welfare. To do its job it is often required to work hand in glove with law enforcement and at times the SA police service. V/O We requested an interview with SPCA Cape of Good Hope as Atlantis and Mamre falls under their jurisdiction. However in an email response CEO Allan Perrins said ‘bush racing may be an urban legend’ . But in this press release of 2013 his office “appealed to the public for assistance in clamping down on bush racing across the province.” Perrins referred us to SPCA Swartland. We spoke to their chairperson, Colette Mang. John Webb: I am not quite understanding why the SPCA does not seem keen on admitting that racing is an issue. Colette Mang: Oh it is an issue and we are totally opposed to racing but you have the racing, in order to fix that let's try and fix the cause. The other problem we had is we had our inspectors threatened. Our senior inspector had to to euthanize a horse and the gang member said to him I know who you are and I know where you stay. Now that is a scary thing to hear. Link: The Mamre flower festival is held every September and is built as a fun filled day out for the entire family but as we discovered, it also has a sinister side. V/O With the drone camera we were able to survey the territory. As the day progressed several groups of riders were warming up and gathering in the nearby fields. From the main road into Mamre, riders from Atlantis were entering. It was clear to us that the local community were accustomed to sharing the roads with the horses as they gave way to the animals. Schaap was at the flower show. Alma Shaap: Animal Welfare: We could see the activity of the horses right near our stall, so close were they and it was mind blowing that where people were parking their cars, where children were walking, literally 60 horses would just come past you speeding in the road. Link: Come late afternoon this stretch of the road was turned into an impromptu race course. We captured footage of two races but then was spotted by scouts and had to beat a hasty retreat. V/O From the sky we could see no visible or definitive starting point or even a winning post. Over a stretch of about 4000 meters several riders were competing pushing their horses hard and fast. Here you can see one of the riders trying to pull his opponent off his horse. Bush racing lasts several days and when the horses can no longer perform, they are simply dumped. John Webb: If it is that obvious that these races are happening why is the SPCA does not follow up? Colette Mang: Yeah because we are a very small SPCA (long pause) we would need help. we haven't had a lot of support from Law enforcement. V/O We put this to the deputy chief of Law Enforcement for the City of Cape Town. John Webb: We have hear from people of the SPCA that if they do ask for intervention form law enforcement they don’t get a lot of support to bush racing in particular. Leon Wentzel: Acting Deputy Chief Law Enforcement: City of Cape Town With regards to bush racing as indicated, it is actually the first time we have encountered this or heard about it. John Webb: If it is that obvious to us why is it not obvious to other people particularly law enforcement? Leon Wentzel: All the dockets throughout the city gets processed by my officer, thus far it is the first time we encounter something like this. V/O Back at Mamre, our drone circled the sky and on the ground parked on the ground parked at the bush race was a police vehicle, the occupants engaging in a conversation with one of the riders. They did not appear to make any effort in investigating what was clearly an illegal activity taking place. John Webb: Another worrying aspect is that there are law enforcers present at these events. That is obviously something you will investigate? Leon Wentzel: That would be and I will definitely initiate an investigation. We do not take it lightly when officers turn a blind eye to any contravention or where the safety of the public is concerned. V/O Garth has become a strong supporter of animal rights and has spent more time in contributing to rescue missions with his drone. Garth Malpass: The more I got into it the more emotional i got an the more I wanted to find these horses and the more I wanted to assist with. V/O Of the two retired racehorses that were rescued over that Easter Weekend by Garth and his the team one did not make it. Max’s injuries was so severe that he was put to sleep. ___________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ Promos: 10 seconds: V/O Bush racing is an inhumane sport organised by gangsters with total disregard for the welfare of the animal. 15 seconds: V/O This is bush racing, a sport organised by gangsters who race the animals into the ground. Mayanna Muter: The injuries, a lot of them have these massive wounds on their backs from constant friction, they have stab wounds, one horse was actually sliced. 15 seconds: V/O In bush racing stolen horses are raced to their death. Garth Malpass: Not only was it a broken leg, it was exhausted, it was shaking so much as if it wanted to fall over. Jennifer Deverson: These horses are just ridden until they can't go any more. ________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ Invoicing Back references from Insert ID in Invoice: Title Author Last Updated Invoice for Bush racing (5095) Annalise Lubbe 10 October 2017

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): It is known as bush riding - a brutal and inhumane sport organised by gangsters that forces retired racehorses to run themselves literally to death. Carte Blanche investigates.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Retired race horses are forced to run beyond their limits on tar roads, often around blocks of houses leading to severe animal cruelty and abuse. Controlled by gangs and suspected ringleaders the sport of bush racing has been difficult to crack down by law enforcement. The SPCA lacks the funds and so this inhumane sport continues to grow in the Western Cape amongst the coloured communities.
metadata.Summary: It was the Wednesday before Easter Weekend. When most families were getting ready to celebrate this special time of the year, Michael Brand was in a state of anxiety. He bought a horse from Jenny Middleton who runs a rehoming centre for retired race horses in Phillip on the Cape Flats last Saturday. Max was a six year old mare in good shape and there was an immediate bond between the two. Michael was eager to fetch Max that Saturday. But then his plans went astray when he got a call from Jenny saying that Max was missing. The fence of the property was cut and both Max and another horse, named Wavin Flag was taken. Jenny’s immediate fear was that the horses were stolen for bush racing. With a large bush racing meeting scheduled for the Cape Flats over easter weekend, fears ran high that the horses had been stolen for illicit racing. Michael got onto social media and with the news shared on various platforms and the help of SAPS stock theft unit, a PI and drone surveillance footage Max and Wavin Flag was eventually found on Easter Friday in the dunes of Rocklands near Mitchells Plain. The recovery team was surrounded by a fairly hostile crowd of people leading to further speculation that the racing might have been linked to gangs who run the horses for bets, akin to cock fighting and dog figiting rings. When Michael saw Max his fears were confirmed. “Max could not even get into the horse box by himself, it took 10 of us to load him in,” he remembers. Back at the centre Jenny was waiting with a vet to attend to the animals. “They’d obviously been galloped into the ground” says Jenny as their mouths had wires through them and were bleeding and you could see straightaway that Max’s leg did not look good.” X Rays revealed that Max had sustained serious injuries, including fracturing his sesamoids beyond repair and due to the extent of his injuries the decision was made to euthanise him humanely.
metadata.Further information: Michael still gets choked up when he thinks about what Max must have gone through. This is the story of so many cases involving bush racing - a secretive sport that has been difficult to crack down. The sport has become a highly lucrative pastime for weekends and public holidays and is rife across the coloured communities of the Western Cape. The location is kept a secret till the last moment to ensure no unwanted parties will interfere as horses are often stolen and shows signs of severe animal abuse. It is known that this form of sport puts horses through the most severe tests in order to win the race. There are no rules, no regulations, only the prize money at stake for the winner. The horses are transported in the most inhumane way. Tied by ropes they are stacked on top of another at the back of a bakkie and taken to the location. Once at the race, no proper equipment is used. Instead, a wire bit in the mouth for control, a shambock or teaser for speed, and bare-back riding, causing severe friction and sores in the process. And the racecourse? The veld or a backstreet tar road filled with litter and debris causing major injuries in the horse’s hooves. Evidence of this is found in a veterinary report from Dr. John Midgley from Atlantis area when he examined a severely traumatised horse that was found after a bush race that came in with multiple injuries. She had open sores, bruises on her back and abscesses on her hooves. ‘The abscess on her hooves is from working at speed for an extended period of time on hard surfaces such as tar roads,” Midgley stated. And when a horse is no longer able to run, the owners simply abandon the animal in the veld left to die. Alma Schaap from African Tails, who works with the communities of the Swartland area through offering animal rescue services will tell you how often she has been called by a local community member who found a dead horse close to where bush racing has taken place. Alma has held workshops with the community members where she tried to install a sense of responsibility towards the horse’s welfare. It has been a long journey and she has seen some results but in most cases the abuse is at the hands of gangsters who simply don’t care, she states. What concerns her is that very little has been done by the authorities over the years. She has on numerous occasions informed the SPCA about a bush race in their area when she hears about it via an informer but no real action has been taken she feels, not by them nor by SAPS in trying to rescue these animals from severe abuse. Often it is a case of not enough manpower and a lack of funds they say. And when you ask about where the horses come from, Alma will tell you that are either stolen or sold by a local farmer in the Swartberg, called Visser. He drops off a bunch of horses every now and then in Mamre and these people buy a retired racehorse for as little as R500, she says. Alma works closely with equestrian community who has helped with rescue horses in building them up to strength again. Anushka, seen by Dr. Midgley was a worse case scenario that took 6 months to heal from open sores and injuries she sustained in races. Today she is at a happy home and shows new life again. But so many of these horses are not rescued in time and the spiral of abuse continue. Our story: Through the eyes of Michael we will hear about Max’s story in Mitchells Plain and show the drone footage of the rescue mission. There is also supporting go-pro visuals of Max at the rehoming centre and some of the team members who worked together during the rescue mission. A visit to the heart of the Swartland, Atlantis, Pella and Mamre, where many of these events are held over weekends will form part of our story. You only need to visit the coloured community of Mamre to spot a horse in the backyard that is severely neglected to know what his purpose is, as Alma will testify. We will send a drone camera into the town of Mamre this weekend during the annual flower show as there is a planned race on the Saturday we were told. We hope to get aerial visuals of this event as it is virtually impossible for one of us to get ground visuals during the event without putting our lives at risk. The race is 100% coloured community attending. We aim to find Farmer Visser and see if he will speak to us about the horses he sells to the coloureds for bush racing. If we are able to get one of the locals who bought a horse from farmer Visser the story will be stronger. We will get a spokesperson of the SPCA and Law Enforcement representative to talk to us about what action they have taken and how they intend to stamp out bush racing. The veterinary report and an interview with the Dr. will form part of the evidence of one of the horses, Anuschka, who is now in good hands and recovering. This I feel is also important for our viewers to feel it is not all doom and gloom but that there is a shimmer of hope for those horses that are rescued. In closing, this is an extremely difficult story to get ground visuals of so most of the evidence will be from drone footage as well as a cellphone recording of a race given to us by someone from the horse cart association who cannot go on camera as she fears for her safety.
